summary: Documents a MIB for use with CMIP, either over OSI stacks or with CMIP over TCP, redefining MIB-II objects to fit the OSI structure of management information. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: It rewrites a checklist of network facts in the style of another family of standards that is no longer used.

subtitle: Adapting TCP/IP network management to OSI standards

tldr.problem: TCP/IP networks needed a management information base (MIB) that worked with OSI-based management protocols (CMIP), not just SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC reformats the existing MIB-II into OSI templates and structures, adding attributes for object identification and events compatible with the OSI management protocol.
tldr.outcome: The document is Historic; it was superseded as OSI management did not achieve widespread adoption and SNMP remained the dominant network management approach.

today: RFC 1214 is Historic. It was designed for use with CMIP and OSI management protocols, which never achieved significant deployment in TCP/IP networks. SNMP and its successors (SNMPv2, SNMPv3) became the standard management approach instead.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1214 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for use with the OSI network management protocol in TCP/IP-based internets. It takes the existing MIB-II specification and reformats it using OSI templates, then adds attributes necessary for identification and use with the OSI management protocol (CMIP).

The document was created because while SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) became the TCP/IP standard for network management, some organizations wanted to use OSI management frameworks instead. This RFC provides a bridge by defining how to represent the same network management information in OSI style.
sections.plainLanguage: Different teams have different ways of organizing information. This explains how to write the same network device checklist in the OSI way instead of the SNMP way.

sections.title: Structure and Additions to MIB-II
sections.content:
The OSI version of the MIB includes all objects from MIB-II without changing their registered identifiers or behavior, but reformats them into OSI object classes and attributes. New additions include:

  • A root managed object class called top, inherited by all OSI management objects
  • Distinguished names for identifying specific instances of managed objects in the containment hierarchy
  • Events (notifications) including cold start, warm start, link up, link down, and authentication failure events
  • Name bindings that define how objects relate to each other in the naming tree

The containment tree begins with root, with the system object as its child, and agents may ignore relative distinguished names that precede the system object.
sections.plainLanguage: It adds a family tree for network objects, special names to find them, alerts when things happen, and rules for how objects fit together.

sections.title: Object Classes and Organization
sections.content:
The document converts MIB-II components into OSI managed object classes. MIB-II groups (system, interfaces, IP, TCP, UDP, etc.) become object classes. Tables become object classes, and table entries become separate object classes. All other MIB-II object types become OSI attributes assigned to the appropriate classes.

For example, the system class includes attributes like system description, object ID, uptime, contact, name, location, and services. The interfaces class contains interface count and interface ID. Network protocol objects like ip, tcp, and udp each become their own classes with attributes for traffic statistics and configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Network devices are organized into groups (system info, network interfaces, protocols) with each group having a list of measurable details you can check.

sections.title: Attributes and Naming Conventions
sections.content:
Each managed object class has attributes defined with ASN.1 syntax. Attributes have names like sysDescr, ifSpeed, or tcpCurrEstab, and are specified with whether they support reading (GET), reading and writing (GET-REPLACE), and matching operations like equality or ordering.

For object instance identification, distinguished names consist of a sequence of relative distinguished names down the containment path. Object classes with single instances normally use an empty string as the naming attribute value. Table entries use naming attributes compatible with SNMP instance identification conventions, allowing a common API to work with both CMIP and SNMP.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece of information has a name and rules for who can look at it or change it. Objects are found by following a path from the root, similar to how folders organize files.

sections.title: Notifications and Management Events
sections.content:
The RFC defines events (also called notifications) that occur during network operation. These are assigned to specific object classes: the system class receives cold start and warm start events, interface entries receive link up and link down events, the SNMP group receives authentication failure events, and EGP neighbor entries receive neighbor loss events.

Events are defined according to the OSI Structure of Management Information (SMI). The SNMP-defined events are reused here and assigned to specific object classes, since the OSI SMI requires that notifications be part of specific managed object definitions rather than global.
sections.plainLanguage: The system can send alerts when it starts up, when network cables are plugged or unplugged, or when something tries to snoop without permission.

sections.title: Compatibility and Status Today
sections.content:
The document incorporates updates from RFC 1158 (the successor to the original MIB-II RFC 1156) and maintains full compatibility with existing MIB-II semantics and registered object identifiers. It uses ASN.1 templates defined in ISO/IEC 10165 standards for OSI management.

RFC 1214 is Historic because OSI-based network management never achieved significant deployment. SNMP and its variants (SNMPv2, SNMPv3) became the dominant network management standard in TCP/IP networks instead. The document remains useful as a historical reference for how MIB-II was adapted to OSI frameworks, but implementations are no longer recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: This tries to use OSI (an older type of network standard) instead of SNMP. OSI never became popular, so this approach was abandoned in favor of the simpler SNMP method.
